newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak SIS involved in anti-Kovac campaign-agent.
newsitem.headline: Slovak SIS involved in anti-Kovac campaign-agent.

text.p: A man claiming to be an agent of the Slovak intelligence service, the SIS, told a Bratislava radio station on Tuesday that the 1995 kidnapping of the son of President Michal Kovac was orchestrated by the SIS.

In an interview with the independent Radio Twist, Michal Patrik said he had been hired by the SIS to manipulate facts on the case of the kidnapping of Michal Kovac Junior, which has been shelved by the police.

Patrik said un-named senior SIS officers had forced him to record a video-tape in which he claimed the kidnapping was faked and that the leading opposition party, the Christian Democratic Movement (KDH), has been involved in the fake.

"I recorded this statement because I was under pressure and mental duress from SIS officers... My entire work (in SIS) was aimed at discrediting both the president and his son," he said adding that he asked for a 15 million crown ($450,000) payment for the job.

Kovac Junior was kidnapped in August 1995, forced to drink a large amount of alcohol, bundled into the boot of his car and dumped outside a police station in Austria where there was an outstanding international warrant for him on charges of fraud. He was later released by a Vienna court.
The radio said Patrik had provided it with evidence supporting his claim that he was an SIS agent. The information has yet to be independently confirmed.
The issue remains highly-charged in Slovakia with the opposition and part of the media attributing the kidnapping to a feud between Kovac and Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar.
Two senior police detectives were sacked after their investigation led them to suspect SIS involvement in the kidnapping.
A former SIS member, Oskar Fegyveres, now in hiding, told both investigators the abduction was organised by SIS chief Ivan Lexa, a close ally of Meciar.

Fegyveres' confession was later countered by a man claiming to have taken part in faking the entire kidnapping of Kovac Junior. "This man was an SIS agent whom I know personally," Patrik said, adding that the man had received a car, new flat and a loan to open a sex club as a reward for his testimony.

Last October U.S. ambassador to Slovakia Ralph Johnson warned that Bratislava would harm its chances of joining NATO and the European Union if it failed to clear up a tangled set of criminal cases with political links.
The third investigator working on the case, Major Jozef Ciz, who shelved the abduction case, said he saw no reason to reopen the investigation, as Patrik has so far not been interrogated.
"I consider some media information irrelevant, as it can have only an advisory value," Ciz told Radio Twist.
